title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback
extended_summary:
This study examined whether AI-generated feedback could match instructor feedback in an authentic programming course setting, and how students perceived and used each type of feedback. The core question was not only whether students liked the feedback, but whether they could use it to improve their work. The authors focused on usefulness, fairness, developmental value, and encouragement as perception dimensions, and on actual score improvement as the behavioral outcome.

The intervention took place in an undergraduate Java programming course at a public university in Türkiye. Students were randomly assigned to receive either instructor feedback or ChatGPT-4-generated feedback on a lab exam submission. Both conditions used the same rubric, and both kinds of feedback were written to provide hints and explanations rather than direct solutions. Students then revised their submissions during a supervised feedback session and completed a perception questionnaire afterward. The study also controlled for prior knowledge using midterm scores.

Results showed that students viewed both feedback sources positively, but instructor feedback was rated significantly more useful. Although instructor feedback was also rated higher on fairness, developmental value, and encouragement, those differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, students receiving instructor feedback improved their lab scores significantly more than those receiving AI feedback, even after controlling for prior knowledge. The authors conclude that current LLM-based feedback may need stronger educational-context grounding and that hybrid human–AI feedback models are likely to be more effective than AI alone.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used to generate natural-language feedback from prompts and uploaded files.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI feedback provider for students' Java lab submissions. The study uploaded the same rubric, lab instructions, and student Java file to ChatGPT 4 and used one fixed prompt to produce feedback that mirrored the instructor's plain-language, hint-based feedback style.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 35 analyzed students (18 instructor-feedback, 17 AI-feedback), students receiving ChatGPT-generated feedback reported significantly lower usefulness than those receiving instructor feedback. The Mann-Whitney U test found a difference for usefulness (U=191.0, p=0.04), while fairness, development, and encouragement were not significantly different.

After controlling for midterm scores, students receiving ChatGPT-generated feedback improved less on their Java lab resubmissions than students receiving instructor feedback. The robust ANCOVA showed a significant group effect (coefficient=-4.97, SE=2.40, t=-2.07, p=0.04), indicating lower score gains for the AI-feedback group.
findings.measure: Change in lab assignment scores from initial to revised submission

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with between-subjects assignment and a controlled comparison of AI versus instructor feedback. The study uses clear measures, a pre-specified rubric, and appropriate statistical analyses, though the final analytic sample is small and one ANCOVA assumption was violated and addressed with robust standard errors.
impact_tier_rationale: The study found statistically significant differences, but effect sizes were not reported and the practical magnitude is not directly quantifiable from the paper. The direction suggests AI feedback underperformed instructor feedback, but the evidence supports a negative/uncertain impact rather than a clearly large one.
